blocks.text: A combination is an unordered selection of items, where choosing A, B, C counts as exactly the same result as choosing C, B, A, unlike a permutation where order matters. This distinction, order matters or not, determines which of the two closely related counting formulas actually applies to a given problem.

blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439733789-154190692.png
1. What a Combination Is
A combination selects a subset of items without regard to order, choosing the group {A, B, C} is identical to choosing {C, B, A}, both represent the exact same selection.

code.content:
from itertools import combinations
result = list(combinations(["A", "B", "C", "D"], 2))
print(result)   # every unordered pair chosen from 4 letters

blocks.text: This order-independence is precisely what separates a combination from a permutation, and recognizing which property a real problem actually has is the key first step in choosing the correct formula.
A useful shorthand for remembering the distinction, if rearranging the same chosen items would count as a different answer, use permutations, if it would not, use combinations.
Confirming this rule on a tiny, easy to list example, such as choosing 2 letters from a 3 letter set, builds confidence before applying the formula to larger, harder to enumerate problems.
2. The n Choose r Formula
The number of ways to choose r items from n, ignoring order, is written n choose r, computed as n factorial divided by (r factorial times (n minus r) factorial).

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Choosing 2 items from a set of 4 gives 4 factorial divided by 2 factorial times 2 factorial, which simplifies to 24 divided by 4, exactly 6, matching every listed unordered pair directly.

blocks.text: This notation, n choose r, is read aloud exactly that way, and is also sometimes written as C(n, r) in textbooks and papers.

This same formula reappears throughout probability theory as well, particularly in computing binomial probabilities where the number of ways an event can occur a certain number of times matters directly.
3. Deriving Combinations from Permutations

The n permute r formula from the permutations lesson counts every ordered arrangement of r items, but since each unordered group of r items can itself be arranged in r factorial different orders, dividing n permute r by r factorial removes that duplicate counting, giving exactly the combinations formula.
This derivation is worth remembering directly, rather than memorizing the combinations formula separately, it can always be rebuilt on the spot from the permutations formula whenever needed.

Every combinations formula problem can, in principle, be solved by first counting permutations and then dividing by the redundant orderings, though in practice it is faster to apply the combinations formula directly.
Seeing this derivation once tends to make the combinations formula feel far less arbitrary than simply memorizing it as a standalone rule.
4. A Worked Example: Choosing a Committee
From a group of 10 people, how many different 3-person committees can be formed, where the order people are selected in does not matter?

If instead the problem had asked for a specific president, secretary, and treasurer role assignment, order would matter and the permutation formula, not this combination formula, would be the correct one to use.
Notice how much smaller 120 is compared to the corresponding permutation count for the same numbers, reflecting how many duplicate orderings the combinations formula correctly removes.

Committee selection is one of the most classic textbook examples specifically because it makes the order-independence property so intuitive, a committee membership list does not care what order the members were chosen in.
5. Symmetry: n Choose r Equals n Choose (n minus r)
Choosing r items to include is mathematically identical to choosing n minus r items to leave out, so n choose r always equals n choose (n minus r), a useful symmetry for simplifying calculations.
This symmetry can meaningfully simplify hand calculations, choosing 7 out of 10 committee members is exactly as many ways as choosing which 3 to leave out instead.
This property also gives a quick sanity check, if a calculated n choose r value does not match its mirrored n choose (n minus r) counterpart, an arithmetic mistake has likely been made somewhere.
Applying this shortcut whenever r is closer to n than to 0 keeps the factorial values involved as small and manageable as possible.
6. Pascal's Triangle

Pascal triangle arranges the n choose r values in a triangular grid, where each entry equals the sum of the two entries directly above it, giving a fast way to compute combination values without factorials for small n.

This same triangle appears throughout mathematics well beyond combinatorics, including in the binomial theorem for expanding powers of a sum, a connection worth knowing exists even without deriving it here.
Each row of the triangle sums to a power of 2, another elegant property connecting combinations directly to binary counting, worth knowing exists even without proving it here.
Building a few rows of the triangle by hand is a fast way to double check a computed combination value without needing a calculator at all.
7. Combinations in Feature Selection

Choosing which subset of features out of a larger set to use in a model is a combinations problem, the number of possible feature subsets of size r out of n total features grows according to exactly the n choose r formula.

With 20 candidate features, choosing subsets of size 5 already gives over 15000 possible combinations to consider, illustrating why exhaustive feature subset search quickly becomes impractical without a smarter search strategy.

Exhaustively evaluating every possible feature combination is called subset selection, and it quickly becomes computationally infeasible past a modest number of candidate features, motivating greedy or randomized alternatives instead.
Wrapper based feature selection methods, which repeatedly train and evaluate a model on different feature subsets, are directly bounded by this same combinatorial explosion.
8. Combinations in Cross Validation

Some cross validation schemes explicitly enumerate all possible ways to split a dataset into training and validation groups of specified sizes, a direct application of the combinations formula to count how many such splits exist.
Leave-p-out cross validation, which tests every possible way of holding out p data points, is a direct, literal application of the combinations formula to enumerate every validation split.

This approach becomes computationally expensive quickly as dataset size grows, which is why k-fold cross validation, a much smaller, structured subset of all possible splits, is used far more often in practice.
Understanding leave-p-out as a combinations problem also explains directly why it becomes computationally infeasible so quickly as p or the dataset size grows.
9. Combinations With Repetition

When items can be chosen more than once, such as selecting 3 scoops of ice cream from 5 flavors where repeats are allowed, a different formula applies, called combinations with repetition, computed as (n plus r minus 1) choose r rather than the standard n choose r.
The plus r minus 1 term in this formula accounts for the extra freedom repetition introduces, effectively treating repeated choices as additional slots to distribute among the original n categories.
Ice cream scoop selection is a classic teaching example for this formula specifically because repetition, choosing the same flavor more than once, is such a natural, intuitive scenario to picture.
10. Generating Combinations in Code
Python itertools.combinations directly generates every possible unordered selection of a given size, useful for small sets where exhaustively checking every subset is still computationally feasible.

code.content:
for combo in combinations(["A", "B", "C", "D"], 2):
    print(combo)   # prints all 6 unordered pairs one at a time

blocks.text: For larger sets, the total number of combinations can still grow very large even though it is always smaller than the corresponding permutation count for the same n and r.
For larger sets, generating every combination explicitly becomes impractical, exactly the same scaling concern the permutations lesson raised for exhaustive permutation generation.
11. A Worked Example
A lottery draws 6 numbers from a pool of 49. How many different possible winning combinations are there?
Nearly 14 million possible combinations explains directly why winning this kind of lottery by chance alone is so improbable for any single ticket purchased.
This same style of calculation applies directly to any raffle, lottery, or random draw scenario where a fixed number of items are selected from a larger pool without regard to order.
12. Common Mistakes

items: Using the combination formula when order actually does matter, in that case the permutation formula is the correct one to use instead.
Forgetting the symmetry property, n choose r equals n choose (n minus r), leading to unnecessarily large factorial calculations that could have been simplified.
Confusing n choose r with n permute r, the combination formula includes an extra division by r factorial that the permutation formula does not.
Assuming combinations always involve small numbers, as the lottery example shows, the count can grow into the millions or more even for modest values of n and r.

blocks.text: A related trap worth naming directly: applying the plain combinations formula to a problem that actually allows repeated selections, when the combinations-with-repetition formula from section 9 is the one that applies instead.
It is also easy to forget the symmetry property from section 5 and compute a much larger factorial than necessary when a smaller, mirrored calculation would have given the identical answer.
13. Practice: Count Combinations
A pizza shop offers 8 toppings, and a customer can choose any 3 of them. How many different 3-topping pizzas are possible?
Try the same calculation allowing repeated toppings as well, using the combinations-with-repetition formula, and compare how much larger that count is than the no-repeats version.
This pizza topping scenario is a natural, everyday example of an unordered selection, choosing pepperoni then mushroom results in the exact same pizza as choosing mushroom then pepperoni.
Key Takeaway

A combination counts unordered selections, computed with the n choose r formula, directly derived from the permutation formula by dividing out the r factorial orderings each unordered group could otherwise be arranged in. Order not mattering is the single defining feature separating combinations from permutations.

The logic lesson immediately ahead shifts from counting problems to the foundations of propositional reasoning, the boolean logic that underlies conditional statements, decision boundaries, and filtering operations throughout applied programming and machine learning.

Pascal triangle and the combinations-with-repetition formula, covered in sections 6 and 9, are the two most useful extensions to keep in mind once the basic n choose r formula is comfortably understood.

Feature subset selection and cross validation splitting, covered in sections 7 and 8, show that combinations are not just an abstract counting exercise, they show up directly in everyday machine learning workflow decisions.
